title: The Hermit of the Hind: Athens to Saint-Gilles-du-Gard
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: Athens: Noble Birth and the Flight from Fame

stops.name: Athens, the house of Theodore and Pelagia
stops.campa: Aegidius is born in Athens to Theodore and Pelagia, of royal Greek blood, in the city where the schools still murmur. The boy is given to letters early: Scripture first, then the wisdom of the Greeks, and he surpasses his masters in both. Grace sits on him visibly, the way light sits on marble. The city that once crowned philosophers watches a different kind of philosopher grow: one who will spend his learning like his inheritance, all of it, on God and the poor.
suggested_refs: The Acropolis of Athens, the city of his birth in the vita

stops.name: Athens, the church porch: the cloak laid on the beggar
stops.campa: Going to church, the young Giles finds a sick beggar lying in the way, asking alms. Giles has no coin on him; he unclasps his cloak and lays it over the shivering man. The moment the cloth settles, health returns to the beggar entire; he stands, whole, in a nobleman's coat. The city talks of nothing else. Giles understands, with something like dread, what the garment has told him: that power has been laid on him, and that fame will now hunt him like hounds.
stops.quote: He found a sick man which lay all sick in the way and demanded alms of Saint Giles, which gave him his coat. And as soon as he clad him withal he received full and entire health.
suggested_refs: The cloak miracle in the Legenda Aurea cycle of Saint Giles

stops.name: Athens, the serpent-bitten man and the demoniac
stops.campa: The signs multiply against his will. A man swollen with serpent's venom is carried to Giles; at his prayer the poison withdraws like a tide. In the church a demoniac howls through the psalms until Giles conjures the spirit out of him, and the man stands quiet in the sudden silence. Each cure is a trumpet announcing him to Athens. He begins to look westward, toward some country where nobody knows his name, not understanding yet that his name will follow him across the whole sea.
suggested_refs: Legenda Aurea cycle: the healing miracles of the young Aegidius

stops.name: Athens, the renunciation: the inheritance scattered
stops.campa: Theodore and Pelagia die, and their whole estate falls to their son: houses, lands, gold, the accumulated weight of a royal line. Giles makes Christ his heir. He opens the doors and scatters everything to the poor of Athens until nothing remains that a thief would stoop for. What he keeps is exactly what he gave the beggar: nothing. Stripped of patrimony and famous precisely for having renounced fame, he sees only one road left open: the sea.
suggested_refs: The renunciation scene in the Vita sancti Aegidii

stops.name: Piraeus, the ship west
stops.campa: At the old harbor of Athens, Giles takes passage on a ship bound west, telling no one who he is. Behind him the city that made him; ahead, a coast he has never seen and a language he does not speak, which is precisely the point. He carries no goods and pays with what he is not: he boards as a poor Greek among merchants. The ropes are cast off. The last miracle he leaves Athens is his absence.
suggested_refs: The harbor of Piraeus

stops.name: The open sea off Sicily, the storm calmed
stops.campa: Mid-passage the sky closes and the sea stands up. The mariners, who know exactly what such a sea does to such a ship, cry out for their lives; the mast groans, the water comes over. Giles kneels on the streaming deck and prays. The wind falls out of the sails like a bird shot dead; the swell flattens; the tempest simply ceases. The sailors, dripping and alive, look at their silent Greek passenger and understand what they have been carrying. They set course for Provence and thank God the whole way.
stops.quote: He made his prayer, and anon the tempest ceased.
suggested_refs: The calming of the storm in the Legenda Aurea cycle

stops.name: Marseille, the landing
stops.campa: The ship the storm could not sink comes into the old Greek harbor of Marseille, a fitting door: a city Athens founded receives the Athenian. Giles steps ashore into Gaul with the sailors' blessings at his back, the only fare he ever paid them. Provence opens before him: salt lagoons, white stone, a Latin church already thick with saints. He asks the way inland, not to any court or school, but toward wherever holy men are said to be, and the country answers with one name: Caesarius of Arles.
suggested_refs: The Vieux-Port of Marseille, ancient Massalia

segments.name: Provence of the Saints: Arles and the Gardon

stops.name: Arles, the sojourn with Saint Caesarius
stops.campa: Giles comes to Arles and is received by Saint Caesarius, bishop of the city, and here the legend folds time in its hand as a page is folded in a book, for Caesarius has slept since the days of the Goths, and yet in the vita the two saints sit together as living men, and it is true. Two years Giles remains under that roof, the Greek hermit and the Latin doctor, learning the customs of the Gallic church. Caesarius would keep him forever; Giles is already listening for the desert.
suggested_refs: The primatial church of Saint-Trophime, Arles
The relics of Saint Caesarius of Arles

stops.name: Arles, the fever healed
stops.campa: In Arles a man has burned with fever for three years, and no physic touches it. He is brought to the Greek in the bishop's household. Giles prays, and the three-year fire goes out of the man in an hour, the way a lamp is pinched. Again the crowd; again the pointing; again his name in every mouth of a city: the very thing he crossed a sea to escape. By night he slips out of Arles without farewell, upriver, away from roads, into the wild country of the Gardon.
suggested_refs: Legenda Aurea cycle: the fever cured at Arles

stops.name: The Gorges du Gardon, the cave of Veredemus (La Baume Saint-Vérédème)
stops.campa: In the limestone gorge where the Gardon runs green under cliffs, Giles finds Veredemus, a hermit of his own Greek blood, living in a cave above the water. The two anchorites share the rock, the fasts, the psalms said against the cliff-echo. Roots and prayer are the whole economy. Through their intercession the barrenness lifts from the surrounding country and the fields bear again, so that even their hiding feeds the people who cannot find them. It is the happiest arithmetic of the desert: two men subtracting themselves, and the land increased.
suggested_refs: La Baume Saint-Vérédème: the cave-chapel in the Gorges du Gardon, oldest Christian sanctuary of lower Languedoc

stops.name: Collias, the parting of the hermits
stops.campa: Even a cave in a gorge is found. The country folk have learned the path to the two Greeks, and the sick begin to arrive by the river. Giles knows the pattern now: wherever he heals, a road grows. He embraces Veredemus, who will one day, folded forward in his own story, wear the mitre of Avignon, and goes downriver alone, past Collias, toward the Rhône's mouth, seeking a solitude so deep that only God and the animals hold its map.
suggested_refs: The Gardon at Collias, the hermits' river

segments.name: The Vallée Flavienne: The Hind and the Arrow

stops.name: The forest of the Vallée Flavienne, the last solitude
stops.campa: Near where the Rhône loosens into its delta, in the forest of the Vallée Flavienne, Giles finds what he has crossed the world for: a cave behind a thicket of thorn, a clear spring, and no path anywhere. Here no tongue knows Greek and no mouth knows his name. He gives himself to the fasts and the hours; the wilderness closes over him like water over a stone. He believes he has finally escaped his fame. He has, for a while. The forest keeps his secret and prepares his legend.
suggested_refs: The crypt of Saint-Gilles abbey, built over the cave of the hermitage

stops.name: The hermitage, the hind of God
stops.campa: A hind comes out of the forest to the hermit: a fair doe, sent and provisioned by God for exactly this office. At certain hours she comes to the cave and gives the old man her milk, and this is his whole table. The gentle economy runs for seasons: the man prays, the deer arrives punctual as a bell, the forest witnesses. She is not tamed and he is not fed by men; both live directly out of the hand of God, who keeps a creature for every hermit and an hour for every mercy.
stops.quote: A fair hind, which without doubt was purveyed of God for to nourish him, and at certain hours ministered her milk to him.
suggested_refs: Master of Saint Giles, 'Saint Giles and the Hind' (National Gallery, London, NG1419)

stops.name: The thicket, the royal hunt and the hounds that halt
stops.campa: The king's hunt enters the forest: Flavius Wamba, king of the Goths, with hounds and horns and knights. The pack sights the fair hind and runs her hard through the trees; she flies to the feet of the man she nourishes. And at the thicket the hounds stop. They cannot come on; they circle and bay at a hedge of thorn as at a wall of iron, and no huntsman can force them a step nearer. The horns call confusion. Something is in that thicket that dogs may not touch, and the king wants to know what.
suggested_refs: The hunt of Wamba in the Vita sancti Aegidii

stops.name: The thicket, the arrow through the hermit's hand
stops.campa: Next day the hunt returns and rings the thicket. The hind breaks for the cave; a knight, to start her, looses an arrow blind into the thorn. Giles has thrown up his hand to shield the fleeing doe, and the shaft passes through the hand that shields her. The hunters hack a way in and find an old man white-haired at prayer, the hind pressed against him, the arrow in his flesh, and not one word of complaint. Blood on the milk-giver's guardian: in this instant the patron of cripples is made, wounded for a creature, crowned by a wound.
stops.quote: One of the knights drew up an arrow follily for to make it afeard and spring out, but he wounded and hurt the holy man, which ceased not to pray for the fair hind.
suggested_refs: Master of Saint Giles, 'Saint Giles and the Hind' (National Gallery, London, NG1419): the arrow, the doe, the kneeling king

stops.name: The cave, the wound refused healing; the king's awe
stops.campa: King and bishop come humbly now, on foot, to the pierced hermit. They send physicians; he sends them away. He prays instead that the wound never close in this life, keeping the arrow's work as his mortification, for he knows that virtue is made perfect in infirmity. The king returns and returns, drawn as the hounds were held back, and lays treasures at the cave mouth; Giles refuses every coin, then relents only this far: let the gold build a house for monks. The king seizes the answer like a grant of grace.
stops.quote: He prayed our Lord that he might never be whole thereof in his life, for he knew well that virtue should profit to him in infirmity.
suggested_refs: The wounded hand in the iconography of Saint Giles, patron of cripples and beggars

segments.name: The Abbey and the Doors of Rome

stops.name: Saint-Gilles-du-Gard, the abbey rises over the cave
stops.campa: On the king's gold and the hermit's ground, a monastery rises in the Vallée Flavienne: the church set directly over the cave, so that the altar stands above the bed of stone where the hind gave milk. Masons where the hounds bayed; a cloister where the thicket stood. Giles watches the walls go up around his solitude and understands the bargain God has struck with him: the world he fled will now be organized, in ranks and habits, around the very hole he hid in. The place will bear his name when the king's is dust.
suggested_refs: The abbey church of Saint-Gilles-du-Gard; the crypt over the hermit's cave

stops.name: Saint-Gilles-du-Gard, the abbot's staff taken
stops.campa: Long he refuses the office: the man who would not keep a coat will not gladly keep a community. But the king presses and the brothers kneel, and at last Giles takes the abbot's staff in the hand the arrow made holy. The wound governs well: no discipline in the house is harsher than the one the abbot keeps on himself, and none gentler than the one he keeps on others. Monks gather to the rule; the poor gather to the gate; the hind's economy, scaled up, becomes a great house of mercy by the Rhône.
suggested_refs: The abbatial tradition of Saint-Gilles

stops.name: Rome, the Pope's blessing and the cypress doors
stops.campa: The abbot goes to Rome to set his house under Peter. The Pope receives him, grants the abbey its privileges, and gives him a gift of weight: two great doors of cypress, carved with the images of the apostles Peter and Paul. Doors: for the man whose life has been a series of doors closed against fame and opened by God. But cypress doors do not ride pack-mules across the Alps. Giles looks at the gift, and then at the Tiber running yellow past the city, and trusts the carrier that has never failed him.
suggested_refs: Old Saint Peter's basilica, Rome

stops.name: The Tiber, the doors cast on the water
stops.campa: At the river's edge Giles has the cypress doors carried down and thrown into the Tiber, commending them to God for pilot, freight-master and crew. The doors do not sink. They take the current like swans, Peter and Paul face-up to heaven, and go down the river toward Ostia and the open sea while the abbot turns north by land, unburdened. Rome has seen triumphs on that water, but never cargo shipped with pure prayer for a bill of lading. The doors are sailing themselves to Provence.
stops.quote: He threw them into the Tiber at Rome, and recommended them to God for to govern.
suggested_refs: The Tiber at Rome; the legend of the self-sailing doors

stops.name: The gate of the abbey, the doors arrive before the abbot
stops.campa: Down the Tiber, across the whole width of the sea, into the Rhône's mouth and up the channel to the abbey landing: when Giles comes home over the mountains, the cypress doors are waiting for him at the monastery gate, dry-faced, punctual, having beaten him to Provence. The brothers hang them where they docked themselves. Peter and Paul now stand door-keepers to the hermit's cave, and every pilgrim who will ever push through them enters on a miracle before setting foot on the floor.
suggested_refs: The portals of Saint-Gilles-du-Gard, remembered in the great Romanesque west front

segments.name: The Mass of Saint Giles and the Last Days

stops.name: Orléans, the Mass of Saint Giles: the angel and the scroll
stops.campa: The king of the Franks summons the abbot north: Charles, whom the tradition names Charlemagne, for here the vita folds time a second time, holding Goth-king and emperor in one hermit's lifetime, and the fold is true. Charles carries a sin so foul he dare not speak it in any confession. Giles says the Mass for him, and as he prays, the angel of the Lord descends and lays a scroll on the altar with the unspoken sin written out entire, and as the hermit prays on, the writing fades letter by letter until the page is clean. The unconfessable is forgiven; the king weeps like a boy.
stops.quote: The angel of our Lord appeared to him, and laid a schedule upon the altar where the sin of the king was written.
suggested_refs: Master of Saint Giles, 'The Mass of Saint Giles' (National Gallery, London, NG4681)
The Charlemagne window, Chartres cathedral, panel of the Mass of Saint Giles

stops.name: Nîmes, the prince's son raised
stops.campa: Homeward from the king's court, Giles passes through Nîmes on the day the prince's son is carried out dead, the house loud with mourning. The abbot goes in to the body as calmly as to a sleeping guest, prays, and gives the boy back to his father alive: the vita's resurrection, done in a doorway, almost in passing. The man who refused to have his own hand healed spends the great cures freely on others. Nîmes never forgets; the city keeps the story like a relic.
suggested_refs: The resurrection episode in the Vita sancti Aegidii

stops.name: Saint-Gilles-du-Gard, the death of the abbot, 1 September
stops.campa: The abbot announces his death beforehand, as a man names the hour of a ship's sailing, and exhorts the brothers to charity. On the first of September he sleeps and dies goodly in the Lord, above the cave, behind the doors that sailed themselves, the arrow-wound still open in his hand as he had prayed it would be. Many bear witness that they hear the company of angels bearing his soul to heaven: the last fame of the man who fled fame, and this one he cannot escape either. The Church keeps the day forever.
stops.quote: So he slept and died goodly in our Lord. And many witness that they heard the company of angels bearing the soul of him into heaven.
suggested_refs: The feast of Saint Giles, 1 September; the tomb in the crypt of Saint-Gilles

segments.name: The Afterlife of the Tomb: The Fourth Pilgrimage

stops.name: London, St Giles-without-Cripplegate
stops.campa: Outside London's wall, by the gate the lame have made their own, a church of Saint Giles stands from Norman days: St Giles-without-Cripplegate, the crippled patron at the cripples' gate, the plainest sentence the cult ever wrote. Fire and war will take the church again and again; the Blitz will gut it to the shell; and again and again it is raised, indestructible as the legend it serves. Milton will be buried in it. The beggars of every century know the door, and the door, in the manner of Giles's doors, is always there.
suggested_refs: St Giles-without-Cripplegate, Barbican, London
The grave of John Milton

stops.name: Saint-Gilles-du-Gard, the crypt consecrated by Pope Urban II
stops.campa: Four centuries on, the tomb has become a nation of the road. Pope Urban II, fresh from preaching the Crusade at Clermont, comes in person to consecrate the altar of the great new abbey church rising over the hermit's cave. Saint-Gilles is now named the fourth pilgrimage of Christendom, after Jerusalem, after Rome, after Compostela, and the crypt where the abbot lies is a stone harbor for ten thousand crutches. The cripples come to the crippled saint, and the wounded hand, still open in eternity, receives them all.
suggested_refs: The crypt of Saint-Gilles, one of the largest of Christendom
Pope Urban II's consecration, 1096

stops.name: Oxford, St Giles' Church at the north gate of the town
stops.campa: At the edge of Oxford, where the town frays into fields, for Giles's churches keep to the margins, the gates, the places where travelers and the poor wash up, a church is consecrated in his name about the year 1120. The broad street before it takes his name too, and once a year erupts into St Giles' Fair around his September feast, the whole city trading and rejoicing on the hermit's doorstep, exactly the tumult he fled and exactly the abundance he fed to others. England will count over a hundred and fifty ancient churches under his name.
suggested_refs: St Giles' Church, Oxford
St Giles' Fair, held around the feast

stops.name: Edinburgh, St Giles' Cathedral on the High Street
stops.campa: The name takes ship as the doors once did. In the days of King David I a church rises on the spine of Edinburgh's rock and is given to the hermit of Provence; it grows into the High Kirk of Scotland, and the Athenian who fled every city becomes the patron of a capital. His arm-bone, they say, comes north as a relic; his hind walks into the city's arms and seals. On the Royal Mile the beggars gather at Saint Giles' door as they gathered at the cave-mouth, and are in the right place.
suggested_refs: St Giles' Cathedral (the High Kirk of Edinburgh)
The burgh arms of Edinburgh with the hind

stops.name: Saint-Gilles-du-Gard, the Romanesque facade and the Via Tolosana
stops.campa: The west front rises: three portals in the Roman manner, apostles ranked in carved stone, one of the glories of Romanesque Provence: the cypress doors of the legend answered at last in marble. Beneath it flows the Via Tolosana, the southernmost road of Saint James, and every pilgrim bound from Arles to Compostela passes through Saint-Gilles as through a needle's eye: they kneel at the hermit's tomb on the way to the apostle's. The abbey stands where the thicket stood, and the road itself is the hind's path, worn continental.
suggested_refs: The west facade of Saint-Gilles-du-Gard
The Via Tolosana (Arles route) of the Camino de Santiago

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, among the Fourteen Holy Helpers
stops.campa: In Franconia a shepherd boy sees the Christ Child ringed by fourteen children of light, who ask a chapel of him: the Fourteen Holy Helpers, and Giles stands among them: the only one of the fourteen who was not a martyr, admitted on the strength of a wound he refused to heal. Where plague and desperation press, his name is invoked against crippling, against terror, against the sin too shameful to confess. The basilica of Vierzehnheiligen will rise on the meadow of the vision, and in its glory of gold and stucco the hermit of the thicket keeps his place, still holding the arrow.
suggested_refs: The Basilica of the Fourteen Holy Helpers (Vierzehnheiligen), Bad Staffelstein
Saint Giles among the Vierzehn Nothelfer
